chunks: Musa ibn al-Qasim from Muhammad ibn 'Umar ibn Yazid from Muhammad ibn 'Udhafir from 'Umar ibn Yazid from Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

Allah the Exalted said in His Book: 'So whoever among you is ill or has an ailment of the head [from fasting] - then ransom is from fasting by day or charity or sacrifice.' So whoever is afflicted with an ailment or pain and uses what is not permissible for the Muhrim when he is healthy, then [the ransom is] fasting for three days, and charity to ten poor people, feeding them from food, and the sacrifice is a sheep which he slaughters, eats from, and feeds [others] from. And indeed, he is only obligated with one of those, so it does not contradict the first report which said in it 'And charity to six poor people, for each poor person two measures,' because the matter in both is optional, because the person is chosen between feeding six poor people, two measures for each poor person, and feeding ten poor people to the extent of their satiety, so there is no contradiction between them in any case, and that which confirms the first narration.

key_terms.مُحْرِمٌ: One in the state of Ihram (pilgrimal consecration)

ai.seo_question: What is the expiation for cutting hair while in Ihram due to illness?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Isfahar clarifies the expiation (kaffarah) for unintentional violations of Ihram prohibitions, such as cutting hair due to illness, by offering three alternative options: fasting, feeding the poor, or sacrificing a sheep. It resolves apparent contradictions in reports regarding the number of poor people to be fed (six vs. ten) by interpreting them as flexible alternatives rather than conflicting obligations, reflecting the Shia scholarly emphasis on ease in ritual law. The text also highlights the principle of choosing one of the three options, ensuring consistency with earlier narrations.
